title: A poem in letters
translation: When Princess Enseimon'in was a little girl, she gave someone who was going to see the retired emperor a poem to pass on as her message:

The letter of two strokes,
the one like an ox's horns,
the straight one, the bent one:
that is how I think of you.
The four letters spell koishiku, "missing you". She was telling him she missed him.
original: {延政門院|えんせいもんゐん}{幼|いときな}くおはしましける{時|とき}、{院|ゐん}へ{参|まゐ}る{人|ひと}に、{御|おん}ことづてとて{申|まう}させ{給|たま}ひける{御歌|おほんうた}、
ふたつ{文字|もじ}{牛|うし}の{角文字|つのもじ}{直|すぐ}な{文字|もじ}ゆがみもじとぞ{君|きみ}はおぼゆる
こひしく{思|おも}ひまゐらせ{給|たま}ふとなり。
literal: When Enseimon'in was young, the poem she had sent, as a message, by a person going to the retired emperor's palace:
'The two(-stroke) letter, the ox's horn letter, the straight letter, the crooked letter: that is how you seem to me.'
It means that she was thinking of him with longing.

notes.text: Princess Etsuko (1259–1332), a daughter of Retired Emperor Go-Saga (the 1925 edition gives the same identification). {門院|もんゐん} is an honorary title given to empresses and princesses.
{院|ゐん}: the retired emperor, usually taken to be her father Go-Saga, who died in 1272, when she was about thirteen.

notes.quote: ふたつ文字牛の角文字直な文字ゆがみもじ
notes.text: A riddle in the shapes of kana, as they were written then. The 1925 edition decodes it: the letter of two strokes is こ, the ox's horns are い, the straight letter is し, the bent letter is く. Together: こいしく, 'longingly, missing (you)'. In historical spelling the word is こひしく, as the last sentence writes it. By this time, ひ in the middle of a word was pronounced like い, so the riddle spells the word by its sound.
ぞ … る: ぞ needs the attributive form, so おぼゆ becomes おぼゆる. おぼゆ: 'to seem, to come to mind'. {君|きみ}: 'you', the father.

notes.quote: こひしく思ひまゐらせ給ふとなり
notes.text: まゐらす is humble toward her father, and {給|たま}ふ is respectful toward her: Kenkō is polite to both of them in one verb. となり: 'that is what it means'. Kenkō explains the riddle in one flat line.
